# Heywood cases: negative variances {.unnumbered}

*First raised in [Week 4](../sem/week-04.qmd). Optional.*

## What it is

A **Heywood case** is an impossible estimate: usually a negative error variance, which means a standardised loading above 1 and an R² above 1 for that item. Amos still reports the estimates and warns about the problem in its notes. Check the **Variances** table every time you fit a model.

## Why it happens

A factor with only three indicators is just identified, so its loadings are determined directly by the three correlations among the items. For the first item, the squared standardised loading is

λ<sub>1</sub>² = r<sub>12</sub> × r<sub>13</sub> / r<sub>23</sub>.

Nothing in that formula stops it exceeding 1.

## A worked example

Suppose three items correlate r<sub>12</sub> = .72, r<sub>13</sub> = .63 and r<sub>23</sub> = .40. Then λ<sub>1</sub>² = .72 × .63 / .40 = 1.13, so the standardised loading is 1.06 and the error variance is −0.13. The other two items are fine (loadings .68 and .59). The low correlation between items 2 and 3 forces item 1 to "explain" more than all of its own variance.

## Common causes, and what to do

| Cause | Sign | What to do |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Sampling error: a true variance close to 0 in a small sample | The negative estimate is small, and its confidence interval includes 0 | Report it. Fixing the variance at a small positive value or 0 is common, but say that you did |
| Misspecification: a missing cross-loading or error covariance | Poor local fit; large modification indices near the item | Respecify, with a substantive reason [@kolenikov2012] |
| Too few indicators per factor, or factors that are nearly the same | Two-indicator factors; factor correlations near 1 | Add indicators or reconsider the measurement model |
| Outliers | Large Mahalanobis distances | Screen the data ([Week 8](../sem/week-08.qmd)) |

Do not simply constrain the variance and move on: a Heywood case is information about the model or the data.

## Reading

- @kolenikov2012, on testing whether a negative variance signals misspecification.
